title: Star stuff
hook: Carl Sagan: we are made of star stuff

segments.voice: Yesterday, Einstein and the most beautiful thing we can experience. Your line was the mysterious. Did a familiar face turn out to hold more than you could see? Today, the awe comes right down to your own body. Day one thousand twenty-six.

The nearest object to you right now is probably your own hand. Skin, knuckles, the faint lines on the palm, the blue of a vein at the wrist. It goes everywhere you go, and it is easy to stop seeing it. The astronomer Carl Sagan, in his television series and book Cosmos, said something about what that hand is made of, something that sounds like poetry but was meant as plain fact. We are made, he said, of star stuff.
screen: `THE NEAREST THING: A HAND.` → `A FAMILIAR THING.` → `MADE OF STAR STUFF.`

segments.voice: Sagan's words are paraphrased here, not quoted. First, the claim. In Cosmos, Sagan explained that the nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, even the carbon in an apple pie, were made inside stars. Much of what our bodies are built from was forged in stars and scattered when they died. Second, what that does to distance. Pascal, at the start of last week, looked at the stars and felt the silence of the infinite spaces. Sagan looks at the same stars and sees family. The sky isn't only out there. Some of it is here, in the hand nearest you. Third, the next step. Sagan went further. He said that through us, the cosmos has a way to know itself. The stuff of stars, put together as a person, now looks back up at the stars and wonders where it came from. Fourth, a neighbor's line. The Bible has its own saying about what a person is made of. In Genesis, God tells Adam: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." That's a different teaching, from a different source, and Sagan wasn't quoting it. But some readers hold the two side by side: dust, and star stuff. Both say a person is made of the stuff of the world, and some readers hear in both a call to humility, and to wonder.
screen: `MADE INSIDE STARS` · `THE SKY IS ALSO HERE` · `THE COSMOS KNOWING ITSELF` · `DUST THOU ART` · then, large: `STAR STUFF.`

segments.voice: The practice is to look at your hand. Rest it, palm up, in your lap or on a table. Look at it the way you'd look at something you've never seen. The lines. The color. The pulse, if you can find it at the wrist. Let the thought come once, without forcing it: much of this was made inside stars. Then just keep looking, and breathing. The bell holds the time.
Star stuff. Carl Sagan's phrase for what we're made of: materials made inside stars, now able to look back up and wonder. Today's word.
Your line: star stuff. Every time you wash your hands today, give them one look, and let the line come back. Day one thousand twenty-six.

howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, use Sagan's picture of star stuff as a short contemplation on the body, often looking at a hand or feeling the pulse while recalling where its materials came from.

fork.setup: Carl Sagan looks at a human body. where does he say the calcium in its teeth and the iron in its blood were made?
fork.reveal: Sagan said they were made inside stars, and that we are made of star stuff.

trapdoor: what you thought: star stuff is a poetic way to say you're special.
what it means: by Sagan's account, much of what your body is built from was made inside stars.
what a scholar hears: Sagan pairs the chemistry with a second claim, that through us the cosmos has a way to know itself.

notes: Sagan is paraphrased only (Cosmos is under copyright). The list of nitrogen in DNA, calcium in teeth, iron in blood and carbon in apple pies follows Sagan's own sentence in Cosmos; confirm chapter (believed chapter 9 of the book, 'The Lives of the Stars').
'The cosmos ... a way to know itself' follows Sagan's line in Cosmos (episode 1 / chapter 1); confirm wording of the paraphrase.
'in his television series and book Cosmos' describes the work without dates; outline date (1980) left out under the claims rule.
Genesis 3:19 is set beside Sagan as a neighbor, with a plain statement that they are different teachings; confirm a Christian or Jewish Keeper is comfortable with the pairing.
Teach refers to day 1016 (Pascal) as 'the start of last week'; 1016 opens the week 1016–1022.
